description: We are a team of data-driven space explorers, passionate about bridging the gap between raw scientific information and engaging, educational experiences. We created Red Horizon: Mars Outpost Commander to show that space exploration isn't just about rockets and astronauts; it's about the intricate dance of resource management and the real-world trade-offs that NASA engineers and mission planners grapple with every day.
summary:
Red Horizon tackles the educational gap by grounding all gameplay in real NASA open data, rather than fabricated statistics. We integrated solar flare data from DONKI to model radiation risk, historical Mars surface conditions from the Perseverance MEDA sensor to impact solar power generation, and biological research insights from the OSDR to define life support parameters. This authenticity ensures that when players decide to ration power, leading to reduced life support, or invest in shielding during a solar event, they are experiencing the exact strategic dilemmas faced by NASA mission planners.

This project is essential because it moves beyond passive fact consumption. By allowing young players to experience the real consequences of survival decisions, Red Horizon builds genuine insight into the complexities of human space exploration, inspiring the next generation of engineers and scientists.
details:
Red Horizon: Mars Outpost Commander is an interactive, browser-based mission control and survival simulation designed to teach students ages 7–12 how astronauts and NASA mission planners manage competing resources on Mars.

How It Works

Players step into the role of Outpost Commander at Jezero Crater over a multi-Sol (Martian day) mission. Each Sol follows a structured decision loop grounded in real environmental constraints:

  1. Review Telemetry: Players inspect daily atmospheric, dust, and space-weather telemetry—including Martian temperature swings, dust optical depth ($\tau$), and incoming solar radiation alerts.
  2. Allocate Limited Power: Because Martian dust reduces solar panel efficiency, players have a capped daily wattage budget that must be split across four competing subsystems: Life Support & Electrolysis (oxygen and water recycling), Active Radiation Shielding (protecting crew health during solar storms), OSDR Greenhouse (food production and morale), and Rover Ops (scientific exploration).
  3. Navigate Communication Delays: Players account for the real-world ~14-minute one-way Earth–Mars communication delay by pre-programming autonomous rover commands rather than relying on instant real-time control.
  4. Resolve Mission Dilemmas: At the end of each Sol, players face an operational dilemma (such as rerouting power during a dust storm or prioritizing crop lighting over rover range) where every choice carries a genuine trade-off.

Benefits & Intended Impact

  • Teaches Systems Thinking Over Memorization: Instead of passively reading space trivia, students experience cause-and-effect dynamics—seeing firsthand how saving power today can trigger an oxygen or radiation deficit tomorrow.
  • Accessible Across Age Groups: Two difficulty modes—Cadet Mode (Ages 7–9) with gentler safety margins and an on-screen guide (Advisor Byte), and Commander Mode (Ages 10–12+) with tighter resource constraints—allow younger kids, older siblings, and classrooms to engage at the right level.
  • Zero-Barrier Deployment: Packaged as a single self-contained web file, it runs instantly in any modern desktop, tablet, or Chromebook browser without downloads, logins, or installations.
  • Intended Impact: By translating authentic NASA mission planning logic into approachable play, the project aims to spark lasting curiosity in STEM and help young learners understand the real engineering challenges behind NASA's Moon-to-Mars exploration goals.

Tools, Languages & Data Sources

  • Coding Languages & Web Standards: Built with HTML5, CSS3 (responsive CSS Grid/Flexbox mission-control interface), and vanilla JavaScript (ES6+) for the simulation engine, state management, and dynamic telemetry updates.
  • Software & Development: Engineered as a standalone, dependency-free single-file web application (index.html) compatible with static web hosting platforms like GitHub Pages and Netlify.
    • NASA DONKI (Space Weather Database Of Notifications, Knowledge, Information): Models real solar flares and coronal mass ejections (such as the September 2017 X8.2 flare and May 2024 CME events) to drive radiation risk.
    • Mars 2020 Perseverance MEDA (Mars Environmental Dynamics Analyzer): Provides authentic Jezero Crater temperature ranges and dust optical depth ($\tau$) readings that directly throttle daily solar array output.
    • NASA OSDR (Open Science Data Repository): Informs crew radiation dosimetry limits, hydrogen-rich water-wall shielding mechanics, and Veggie LED plant-growth energy requirements.

Creativity & Key Design Considerations

  • No "Free" Choices: To mirror real aerospace engineering, our team deliberately avoided creating a "safe" default strategy—every power slider adjustment or dilemma choice forces a meaningful compromise between survival, crew health, and scientific discovery.
  • Translating Jargon Through Context: Scientific terms like Sol, optical depth ($\tau$), dosimetry, and electrolysis are explained directly inside the dashboard tooltips and advisor prompts in plain, age-appropriate language.
  • Cognitive Load Balance: Rather than overwhelming young players with dozens of micro-stats, we consolidated outpost survival into three core, interconnected pillars—Power, Life Support (Oxygen/Food), and Radiation Shielding—keeping the interface intuitive while preserving scientific accuracy.
  • Replayability: Randomized weather sequences and branching daily dilemmas ensure each playthrough presents new combinations of dust storms and solar events, encouraging students to experiment with different survival strategies.
